# Lab 6: A Chain of Yes-or-No Questions
## MPS311/439 Machine Learning
**Lesson 6 Lab Session | Core duration: 50 minutes**

## What this lab is for

In the lecture a decision tree chose its cuts by Gini, grew until it memorised the training set, and had its depth chosen on a validation set. Today you do the same in code:

1. find the best first cut on the lumps, check its Gini by hand, and see whether entropy picks the same cut;
2. hold out a validation set from the digits and choose the depth of a tree on it;
3. read what a tree has learned (its diagram and its feature importance), then read the test set once.

Before each step you will see a question. **Write down your own answer first**, then run the code and compare.

Most code is provided. Your job is to fill the blanks `____`, run the cell, and check your result against the **Success check**. At the end there is a short section on how today's lab helps with **Assignment 2**.

## Part 0: Load the lumps and hold out a validation set (8 minutes)

**Goal:** the same lumps and test set as Labs 4 and 5, and a validation set taken from the training set, as in Lesson 3. Today the Core does not use `X_val`: we split it off only so that `X_fit` holds the same 319 lumps as the lecture. With 426 lumps, cross-validation is the better way to choose (Lesson 6 Note, Section 5).

### 0.1 Load and split

**Question first:** we already have a training set (426 lumps) and a test set (143). Why can we not use the test set to choose the depth of a tree?

Fill the blank so that a quarter of the training lumps becomes the validation set.

```python
import numpy as np                                        # numbers and arrays
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                           # plots
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer          # the lumps
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split     # splitting the data
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier          # the model of today

data = load_breast_cancer()                               # 569 lumps, 30 measurements each
X = data.data                                             # the 30 measurements (features)
y = 1 - data.target                                       # sklearn uses 0 = malignant; we want 1 = malignant
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y)     # the same test set as Labs 4 and 5
X_fit, X_val, y_fit, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_train, y_train, test_size=____, random_state=0, stratify=y_train)   # hold out part of the training set
print(X_fit.shape, X_val.shape, X_test.shape)             # fitting part, validation set, test set
```

**Hint:** a quarter, written as a decimal.

**Success check:** `(319, 30) (107, 30) (143, 30)`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```python
X_fit, X_val, y_fit, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_train, y_train, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y_train)
```

If we chose the depth by looking at the test set, the test set would no longer be unseen data, and its accuracy would be too optimistic. The test set is read once, at the end.
:::

## Part 1: The best first cut (11 minutes)

**Goal:** let a tree with one cut find the best first question on two features, compare Gini with entropy, then check the Gini of the cut by hand.

### 1.1 A tree with one cut

Fill the blank so that the tree asks only one question.

```python
X_fit_two = X_fit[:, [0, 1]]                              # two features: mean radius (0) and mean texture (1)
stump = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=____, random_state=0)   # how many questions from root to leaf
stump.fit(X_fit_two, y_fit)                               # try every cut on both features, keep the best
print(stump.tree_.feature[0])                             # which feature the root uses (0 = radius)
print(stump.tree_.threshold[0])                           # where it cuts
```

**Hint:** one question means depth 1.

**Success check:** `0` and `15.045...`: the root asks "mean radius ≤ 15.05?".

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```python
stump = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0)
```
:::

**Entropy instead of Gini.** scikit-learn scores cuts by Gini unless told otherwise. Another common score is **entropy**, $-p\log_2 p-(1-p)\log_2(1-p)$ (Note Section 2). The Note writes $\log$ without a base; the base of the log does not change which cut is chosen. The cell below fits the same one-cut tree, scored by entropy. Run the cell without changing it.

```python
stump_entropy = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, criterion="entropy", random_state=0)   # score each cut by entropy, not Gini
stump_entropy.fit(X_fit_two, y_fit)                       # the same 319 lumps and the same two features
print(stump_entropy.tree_.feature[0])                     # which feature the root uses (0 = radius)
print(stump_entropy.tree_.threshold[0])                   # where it cuts
```

**Success check:** `0` and `15.045...`: entropy picks the same cut as Gini, radius ≤ 15.045. The shape of entropy is very close to that of Gini, so it usually picks the same cut point (Note Section 2). The lecture and this lab use Gini, the default.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Try with AI (if you finish early, or after class)"}
**You want:** to see the shapes of Gini and entropy side by side.

**Tell the AI:** `p` is the fraction of class 1 on one side; Gini is `2 * p * (1 - p)` and entropy is `-p * log2(p) - (1 - p) * log2(1 - p)`.

**Ask:** *"Plot Gini and entropy against p for p from 0.001 to 0.999 on one figure, with axis labels and a legend."*

**Check:** both curves are 0 at the two ends and highest at `p = 0.5`: Gini at `0.5`, entropy at `1`. The heights differ, but the shapes are very close.
:::

### 1.2 Gini by hand

Run this cell without changing it. It counts the lumps on each side of the cut.

```python
left = y_fit[X_fit[:, 0] <= 15.045]                       # labels on the left of the cut
right = y_fit[X_fit[:, 0] > 15.045]                       # labels on the right
print(len(left), left.sum())                              # lumps on the left, and how many are malignant
print(len(right), right.sum())                            # the same on the right
```

Now fill the two blanks with the number of **malignant** lumps on each side, read from the printed counts.

```python
p_left = ____ / len(left)                                 # share of malignant on the left
p_right = ____ / len(right)                               # share of malignant on the right
gini_left = 2 * p_left * (1 - p_left)                     # Gini of the left side
gini_right = 2 * p_right * (1 - p_right)                  # Gini of the right side
weighted = (len(left) * gini_left + len(right) * gini_right) / len(y_fit)   # the score of this cut
print(round(gini_left, 3), round(gini_right, 3), round(weighted, 3))   # left, right, weighted
```

**Hint:** the second number on each printed line.

**Success check:** `228 35`, `91 84`, then `0.26 0.142 0.226`. Before the cut the Gini was 0.468.

**Questions:**

1. The weighted Gini fell from 0.468 to 0.226. What does a smaller weighted Gini say about the two sides?
2. On this cut, the error rate also falls: from 119 / 319 = 0.373 (call every lump benign) to (35 + 7) / 319 = 0.132 (the 35 malignant lumps on the left and the 7 benign on the right are wrong). But in the lecture's widget (20 blue points among 80 grey, Note Section 2), the error rate stayed at 0.200 wherever the cut was. Why? (Look at which class is the majority on each side of a cut.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```python
p_left = 35 / len(left)
p_right = 84 / len(right)
```

1. Both sides are purer: each side is closer to holding only one class.
2. Grey is the majority on both sides of every cut, so both sides predict grey and the same 20 blue points are always wrong: every cut has the same error rate. Gini still falls when a cut makes one side pure.
:::

## Part 2: Choose the depth on a validation set (14 minutes)

**Goal:** with handwritten digits from MNIST, hold out a validation set, try 20 depths, and choose the best one, as Assignment 2 asks. We use the course's MNIST subset of 10,000 images (Lab 4).

### 2.1 Load and split the digits

Run the cell without changing it. It downloads the MNIST subset (about 1.6 MB). The first split is the one from Labs 4 and 5; the second holds out a validation set.

```python
import urllib.request                                     # to download a file
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wayXing/mps311-439-course-materials/main/lecture-slids/lessons/data/mnist10k.npz"
urllib.request.urlretrieve(DATA_URL, "mnist10k.npz")      # 10,000 MNIST images, about 1.6 MB
mnist = np.load("mnist10k.npz")                           # the file holds two arrays, X and y
X_digits = mnist["X"] / 255                               # 784 pixels per image, scaled to 0 to 1
y_digits = mnist["y"]                                     # the digit, 0 to 9
X_digits_train, X_digits_test, y_digits_train, y_digits_test = train_test_split(
    X_digits, y_digits, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y_digits)   # the same test set as Labs 4 and 5
X_digits_fit, X_digits_val, y_digits_fit, y_digits_val = train_test_split(
    X_digits_train, y_digits_train, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y_digits_train)   # hold out a validation set
print(len(y_digits_fit), len(y_digits_val), len(y_digits_test))   # fitting part, validation set, test set
```

**Success check:** `5625 1875 2500`.

### 2.2 Try 20 depths

**Question first:** as the depth grows, what do you expect the training accuracy to do? And the validation accuracy?

Fill the blanks so that the second number printed is the accuracy on the **validation set**.

```python
for depth in range(1, 21):                                # depths 1 to 20
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=0)   # a tree that stops at this depth
    tree.fit(X_digits_fit, y_digits_fit)                  # fit on the fitting part only
    train_acc = tree.score(X_digits_fit, y_digits_fit)    # accuracy on the images it was fitted on
    val_acc = tree.score(____, ____)                      # accuracy on the validation images
    print(depth, round(train_acc, 3), round(val_acc, 3))  # depth, training, validation
```

**Hint:** the two variables made by the second split in 2.1 that end in `_val`.

**Success check:** the first and last lines are `1 0.195 0.195` and `20 1.0 0.771`; the line for depth 15 is `15 0.996 0.781`.

**Questions:**

1. Which depth has the highest validation accuracy? If two depths tie, take the shallower one. Is it at an end of the range 1 to 20?
2. From depth 10 on, the training accuracy keeps rising to 1.0, but the validation accuracy stays between 0.77 and 0.78. In one sentence: what are the extra levels of the tree doing?
3. Suppose you had tried only depths 1 to 8. Which depth would you have chosen, and what should you do next?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```python
    val_acc = tree.score(X_digits_val, y_digits_val)
```

1. Depth 15 (0.781). Depth 16 ties with it; when two depths tie, take the shallower one, the simpler tree. It is in the middle of 1 to 20, so the range is wide enough. (From depth 10 on, all depths are within about 0.01 of each other.)
2. They fit the fitting images more and more exactly without getting better on new images: the tree is memorising (overfitting).
3. Depth 8, the best of those, but it sits at the upper end. Widen the range upwards and choose again.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Try with AI (if you finish early, or after class)"}
**You want:** the training and validation accuracy against the depth, as one figure. Assignment 2 asks for the same figure as an optional extra.

**Tell the AI:** the loop in 2.2 fits a tree for each depth from 1 to 20 and computes `train_acc` and `val_acc`.

**Ask:** *"Change the loop so that it stores train_acc and val_acc in two lists, then plot both lists against the depth on one figure, with markers, axis labels and a legend."*

**Check:** the training line reaches 1.0 by depth 20; the validation line rises to about `0.78` by depth 10 and then stays between `0.77` and `0.78`.
:::

## Part 3: Read a tree, then the test set once (17 minutes)

**Goal:** read what a tree has learned, from its feature importance and from its diagram; then fit the chosen digits tree and read the test set once.

### 3.1 Read the tree

`tree30` is the tree of Note Section 7, so it uses all 30 features of the 426 training lumps. `feature_importances_` gives how much each feature reduced the Gini in total; the values add up to 1. Run the cell without changing it.

```python
tree30 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=0)   # the depth chosen by cross-validation in Note Section 7
tree30.fit(X_train, y_train)                              # all 30 features of the 426 training lumps
importance = tree30.feature_importances_                  # how much each feature reduced the Gini; adds up to 1
order = np.argsort(importance)[::-1]                      # feature numbers, most important first
for i in order[:5]:                                       # the five most important features
    print(data.feature_names[i], round(importance[i], 3)) # name and importance
print("mean radius", round(importance[0], 3), "mean perimeter", round(importance[2], 3))   # two measurements of size
print("correlation of radius and perimeter:", round(np.corrcoef(X_train[:, 0], X_train[:, 2])[0, 1], 3))   # 1 = they move together exactly
```

**Success check:** first `mean concave points 0.717` (the Note rounds it to 0.72), then `worst concavity 0.069`, `worst radius 0.061`, `mean texture 0.034`, `worst area 0.025`; then `mean radius 0.017 mean perimeter 0.0` and `correlation of radius and perimeter: 0.998`.

`small_tree` is the depth-2 tree of Note Section 3, so it uses the 319 fitting lumps of Part 1. Run the cell without changing it.

```python
from sklearn.tree import plot_tree                        # draws a fitted tree as a diagram
small_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0)   # two questions deep, as in Note Section 3
small_tree.fit(X_fit_two, y_fit)                          # the 319 fitting lumps, mean radius and mean texture
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))                               # a wide figure, so the boxes do not overlap
plot_tree(small_tree, feature_names=["radius", "texture"], class_names=["benign", "malignant"], filled=True)
plt.show()                                                # "yes" (True) goes left, "no" (False) goes right
```

**Success check:** the root asks `radius <= 15.045` and has `gini = 0.468`, `samples = 319` and `value = [200.0, 119.0]`, as in 1.2: `value` counts the fitting lumps in a box, benign first, then malignant.

Read the diagram, not the code: a new lump has radius 17 and texture 14. Walk it down the tree from the root, and fill the blank with the tree's call.

```python
my_call = ____                                            # your call from the diagram: 0 = benign, 1 = malignant
print("your call:", my_call, "the tree's call:", small_tree.predict([[17, 14]])[0])   # the tree walks the same lump
```

**Hint:** at each box, "yes" (True) goes left and "no" (False) goes right. Two questions, then read the `class` of the leaf.

**Success check:** `your call: 0 the tree's call: 0`.

**Questions:**

1. In one sentence: what does the `0.717` of mean concave points mean?
2. Write the two questions the lump with radius 17 answered on its way down, with its answer to each. Its radius is large: which question kept it from being called malignant?
3. (If you are short of time, answer this one after class.) Mean perimeter has importance `0.0`, but its correlation with mean radius is `0.998`. Does this show that the perimeter of a nucleus has nothing to do with whether a lump is malignant? Answer yes or no, with the reason in one sentence.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```python
my_call = 0
```

1. Of all the Gini reduction the tree's cuts achieve, 72% comes from cuts on mean concave points: most of the tree's decisions rest on how many dents there are in the edge of the nucleus (Note Section 7).
2. "radius ≤ 15.045?" No, so go right. "texture ≤ 15.82?" Yes, so go left. It lands in the third leaf from the left, `value = [6, 4]`: 6 benign and 4 malignant fitting lumps, mostly benign, so the call is benign. The texture question kept it from being called malignant.
3. No. Radius and perimeter carry almost the same information, so once the tree has asked about one size measurement, a question on the perimeter adds almost nothing, and its importance stays near 0. Feature importance only tells you what this one tree used (Note Section 10, limitation 4).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Try with AI (if you finish early, or after class)"}
**You want:** to see the rectangles of a shallow tree and a deep tree on the two features.

**Tell the AI:** `X_fit_two` holds mean radius and mean texture for the 319 fitting lumps; `y_fit` holds the labels.

**Ask:** *"For max_depth 2 and 10, fit a DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0) on X_fit_two, predict on a grid from 6 to 29 for radius and 9 to 40 for texture, and draw the predicted regions with the points on top, in two plots side by side."*

**Check:** the depth-2 plot has a few large boxes; the depth-10 plot has many small boxes around single points.

### 3.2 The test set, once

Back to the digits: fit the tree with the depth you chose in 2.2, and read the test set once.

```python
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=____, random_state=0)   # the depth chosen in 2.2
tree.fit(X_digits_fit, y_digits_fit)                      # the same fitting part
print(tree.score(X_digits_test, y_digits_test))           # the test set, read once
```

**Hint:** your answer to question 1 of 2.2. Depths 15 and 16 tie there; take the shallower one, 15.

**Success check:** about `0.776`. It is close to the validation accuracy (0.781): both are images the tree was not fitted on, so a small difference is normal.

**Question:** on the same 2500 test images, logistic regression scored 0.908 (Lesson 4) and shrunk QDA 0.861 (Lesson 5). Give one reason, from the lecture, why a tree may do worse on images of digits. (One reason is enough.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
```python
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=15, random_state=0)
```

Each question in a tree looks at one pixel at a time, so its boundaries are horizontal or vertical. A digit is recognised from many pixels together, which a straight boundary (logistic regression) or an ellipse (QDA) can use at once. (Part of the gap also comes from data: the tree was fitted on 5625 images, the other two on all 7500.)
:::

## A. Find the best cut yourself, one level down

Advanced Study 1 of the Note finds the root cut (radius ≤ 15.045). Here you go one level down, so its numbers will not match yours.

**Tasks**

1. Keep only the fitting lumps on the left of the root cut: `inside = X_fit[:, 0] <= 15.045` (228 lumps, 35 malignant). On their mean radius, take every midpoint between two neighbouring distinct values as a candidate cut. For each, compute the weighted Gini of the two sides (weighted within these 228 lumps), and keep the smallest.
2. Do the same for mean texture. Which feature gives the better cut? Fit `DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0)` on `X_fit[:, :2]` and `y_fit`, and check that its left node makes the same cut: node 1 is the left child of the root, so look at `tree.tree_.feature[1]` and `tree.tree_.threshold[1]`.
3. Repeat task 1 with the error rate instead of Gini. Careful: many cuts may tie, and your loop then keeps only the first one. Compare the fewest errors of any cut with the errors of not cutting at all (call all 228 benign). What does it tell you about choosing cuts by the error rate?

::: {.callout-tip title="Ask AI"}
Ask: *"Why does scikit-learn take midpoints between neighbouring distinct values as candidate cuts, instead of the values themselves?"* Check its answer against Advanced Study 1 of the Note.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
`np.unique(x)` gives the distinct values in order; `(values[:-1] + values[1:]) / 2` gives the midpoints. Take the rows with `X_fit[inside, 0]` and `y_fit[inside]`, and divide by 228 (not 319) when you weight the two sides. After the search for radius works, copy it and change the column number to 1 for texture.
:::

**Self-check:** check the weighted Gini values (the cut 13.41 can also be read off the tree in the Note): in the left node, the best radius cut is about `13.405` with a weighted Gini of about `0.218`; for texture the best is about `18.635` with about `0.235`, so radius wins, and the tree's left node uses feature `0` at `13.405`. With the error rate, no cut does better than 35 wrong out of 228, the same as not cutting at all (all 35 malignant lumps called benign): the error rate sees no gain from any cut, but Gini still finds one.
